claim: Hundreds of cytotoxic natural or synthetic lipidic compounds contain chiral alkynylcarbinol motifs.
source: Hundreds of cytotoxic natural or synthetic lipidic compounds contain chiral alkynylcarbinol motifs, but the mechanism of action of those potential therapeutic agents remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the existence of a class of compounds, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The mechanism of action of alkynylcarbinol-containing compounds remains unknown.
source: Hundreds of cytotoxic natural or synthetic lipidic compounds contain chiral alkynylcarbinol motifs, but the mechanism of action of those potential therapeutic agents remains unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The enantiospecific cytotoxicity of numerous terminal alkynylcarbinols involves bioactivation by HSD17B11.
source: Using a genetic screen in haploid human cells, we discovered that the enantiospecific cytotoxicity of numerous terminal alkynylcarbinols, including the highly cytotoxic dialkynylcarbinols, involves a bioactivation by HSD17B11, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) known to oxidize the C-17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to the corresponding ketone.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by genetic screen data.

claim: HSD17B11 is a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR).
source: Using a genetic screen in haploid human cells, we discovered that the enantiospecific cytotoxicity of numerous terminal alkynylcarbinols, including the highly cytotoxic dialkynylcarbinols, involves a bioactivation by HSD17B11, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) known to oxidize the C-17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to the corresponding ketone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSD17B11's classification.

claim: HSD17B11 oxidizes the C-17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to the corresponding ketone.
source: Using a genetic screen in haploid human cells, we discovered that the enantiospecific cytotoxicity of numerous terminal alkynylcarbinols, including the highly cytotoxic dialkynylcarbinols, involves a bioactivation by HSD17B11, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) known to oxidize the C-17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to the corresponding ketone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSD17B11's known enzymatic activity.

claim: Oxidation of dialkynylcarbinols by HSD17B11 generates dialkynylketones.
source: A similar oxidation of dialkynylcarbinols generates dialkynylketones, that we characterize as highly protein-reactive electrophiles.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on biochemical characterization.

claim: Dialkynylketones are highly protein-reactive electrophiles.
source: A similar oxidation of dialkynylcarbinols generates dialkynylketones, that we characterize as highly protein-reactive electrophiles.
evidence: This is a characterization based on experimental data showing protein reactivity.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols covalently modify several proteins involved in protein-quality control mechanisms.
source: We established that, once bioactivated in cells, the dialkynylcarbinols covalently modify several proteins involved in protein-quality control mechanisms, resulting in their lipoxidation on cysteines and lysines through Michael addition.
evidence: This is a finding supported by proteomics data.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols result in protein lipoxidation on cysteines and lysines through Michael addition.
source: We established that, once bioactivated in cells, the dialkynylcarbinols covalently modify several proteins involved in protein-quality control mechanisms, resulting in their lipoxidation on cysteines and lysines through Michael addition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by chemical characterization and proteomics.

claim: Protein modification by bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols triggers protein association to cellular membranes.
source: For some proteins, this triggers their association to cellular membranes and results in endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response activation, ubiquitin-proteasome system inhibition and cell death by apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by imaging and biochemical data.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols result in endoplasmic reticulum stress.
source: For some proteins, this triggers their association to cellular membranes and results in endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response activation, ubiquitin-proteasome system inhibition and cell death by apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by cellular assays and marker analysis.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols activate the unfolded protein response.
source: For some proteins, this triggers their association to cellular membranes and results in endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response activation, ubiquitin-proteasome system inhibition and cell death by apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by analysis of UPR markers.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols inhibit the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: For some proteins, this triggers their association to cellular membranes and results in endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response activation, ubiquitin-proteasome system inhibition and cell death by apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by UPS activity assays.

claim: Bioactivated dialkynylcarbinols cause cell death by apoptosis.
source: For some proteins, this triggers their association to cellular membranes and results in endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response activation, ubiquitin-proteasome system inhibition and cell death by apoptosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by apoptosis markers and caspase inhibition experiments.

claim: Generic lipidic alkynylcarbinols can be devised to be bioactivated by other SDRs, including human RDH11 and HPGD/15-PGDH.
source: Finally, as a proof-of-concept, we show that generic lipidic alkynylcarbinols can be devised to be bioactivated by other SDRs, including human RDH11 and HPGD/15-PGDH.
evidence: This is a proof-of-concept finding supported by experiments with different SDRs.

claim: The SDR superfamily is one of the largest and most ubiquitous.
source: Given that the SDR superfamily is one of the largest and most ubiquitous, this unique cytotoxic mechanism-of-action could be widely exploited to treat diseases, in particular cancer, through the design of tailored prodrugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SDR superfamily.

claim: This cytotoxic mechanism-of-action could be exploited to treat diseases, in particular cancer, through the design of tailored prodrugs.

claim: Marine sponges have attracted pharmaceutical interest since the discovery in the 1950s of C-nucleosides in Cryptotethia crypta.
source: Marine sponges have attracted pharmaceutical interest since the discovery in the 1950s of C-nucleosides in Cryptotethia crypta that led to the development of cytosine arabinoside (ara-C or cytarabine) and analogues as anticancer treatments for acute myelogenous leukemia (Bergmann, 1950; Ellison et al., 1968).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The discovery of C-nucleosides in Cryptotethia crypta led to the development of cytosine arabinoside (ara-C or cytarabine) and analogues as anticancer treatments for acute myelogenous leukemia.
source: Marine sponges have attracted pharmaceutical interest since the discovery in the 1950s of C-nucleosides in Cryptotethia crypta that led to the development of cytosine arabinoside (ara-C or cytarabine) and analogues as anticancer treatments for acute myelogenous leukemia (Bergmann, 1950; Ellison et al., 1968).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Petrocortyne A was isolated from Petrosia sp.
source: In a different structural series, several cytotoxic acetylenic lipids bearing a terminal alkenylalkynylcarbinol (AAC) pharmacophore have since been isolated from marine sponges, such as petrocortyne A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), isolated from Petrosia sp. (Seo et al., 1998) and fulvinol isolated from Haliclona fulva (Ortega et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Fulvinol was isolated from Haliclona fulva.
source: In a different structural series, several cytotoxic acetylenic lipids bearing a terminal alkenylalkynylcarbinol (AAC) pharmacophore have since been isolated from marine sponges, such as petrocortyne A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), isolated from Petrosia sp. (Seo et al., 1998) and fulvinol isolated from Haliclona fulva (Ortega et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: (S)-eicos-(4E)-en-1-yn-3-ol ((S)–1) was isolated from the marine sponge Cribrochalina vasculum.
source: The simplest cytotoxic AAC representative, (S)-eicos-(4E)-en-1-yn-3-ol ((S)–1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was isolated from the marine sponge Cribrochalina vasculum (Gunasekera and Faircloth, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: (S)-eicos-(4E)-en-1-yn-3-ol demonstrated high cytotoxic activity selectively towards non-small cell lung carcinoma cells as compared to normal lung fibroblasts.
source: It demonstrated high cytotoxic activity selectively towards non-small cell lung carcinoma cells as compared to normal lung fibroblasts (Zovko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The non-natural enantiomer (R)–1 has higher cytotoxic activity than (S)–1.
source: Starting from (S)–1, an extensive structure-activity relationship study in human cancer cell lines established that (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): (i) the non-natural enantiomer (R)–1 has higher cytotoxic activity, (ii) homologues with shorter lipidic tails are more cytotoxic, with an optimum total aliphatic backbone of 17 carbon atoms (e.g. (R)–2), and (iii) replacement of the internal C=C bond by a C≡C bond, giving rise to a terminal dialkynylcarbinol (DAC) pharmacophore, further increases cytotoxicity, to reach an IC50 down to 90 nM for the DAC (S)–3 (El Arfaoui et al., 2013; Listunov et al., 2015a; Listunov et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Homologues with shorter lipidic tails are more cytotoxic, with an optimum total aliphatic backbone of 17 carbon atoms.
source: Starting from (S)–1, an extensive structure-activity relationship study in human cancer cell lines established that (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): (i) the non-natural enantiomer (R)–1 has higher cytotoxic activity, (ii) homologues with shorter lipidic tails are more cytotoxic, with an optimum total aliphatic backbone of 17 carbon atoms (e.g. (R)–2), and (iii) replacement of the internal C=C bond by a C≡C bond, giving rise to a terminal dialkynylcarbinol (DAC) pharmacophore, further increases cytotoxicity, to reach an IC50 down to 90 nM for the DAC (S)–3 (El Arfaoui et al., 2013; Listunov et al., 2015a; Listunov et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Replacement of the internal C=C bond by a C≡C bond increases cytotoxicity, reaching an IC50 down to 90 nM for the DAC (S)–3.
source: Starting from (S)–1, an extensive structure-activity relationship study in human cancer cell lines established that (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): (i) the non-natural enantiomer (R)–1 has higher cytotoxic activity, (ii) homologues with shorter lipidic tails are more cytotoxic, with an optimum total aliphatic backbone of 17 carbon atoms (e.g. (R)–2), and (iii) replacement of the internal C=C bond by a C≡C bond, giving rise to a terminal dialkynylcarbinol (DAC) pharmacophore, further increases cytotoxicity, to reach an IC50 down to 90 nM for the DAC (S)–3 (El Arfaoui et al., 2013; Listunov et al., 2015a; Listunov et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The mode of action of the natural compound (S)–1 remains elusive.
source: However, despite this significant level of activity, the mode of action of this family of molecules, including the natural compound (S)–1, remains elusive (Zovko et al., 2014).
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap, supported by citation.

claim: (S)–3 exhibits nanomolar cytotoxic activity in HAP-1 cells with an IC50 of 62.4 nM.
source: We first confirmed in HAP-1 that (S)–3, but not (R)–3 (Figure 1A), exhibits nanomolar cytotoxic activity (Figure 1B, IC50 62.4 nM), in agreement with previous results on HCT116 colon cancer cells (El Arfaoui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: (R)–3 does not exhibit cytotoxic activity in HAP-1 cells.
source: We first confirmed in HAP-1 that (S)–3, but not (R)–3 (Figure 1A), exhibits nanomolar cytotoxic activity (Figure 1B, IC50 62.4 nM), in agreement with previous results on HCT116 colon cancer cells (El Arfaoui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ten individual (S)–3-resistant clones (DACR) were isolated, displaying a 38- to 62-fold resistance to (S)–3.
source: Ten individual (S)–3-resistant clones (DACR) were isolated, displaying a 38- to 62-fold resistance to (S)–3 (Figure 1C) but similar sensitivity as parental cells to two unrelated compounds, bortezomib and doxorubicin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: DACR clones show similar sensitivity as parental cells to bortezomib and doxorubicin.
source: Ten individual (S)–3-resistant clones (DACR) were isolated, displaying a 38- to 62-fold resistance to (S)–3 (Figure 1C) but similar sensitivity as parental cells to two unrelated compounds, bortezomib and doxorubicin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Around nine mutated genes were identified per DACR clone.
source: Based on previous work (Wacker et al., 2012; Bossaert et al., 2021), and considering that EMS induces mainly point mutations under these conditions (Forment et al., 2017), we selected four DACR clones for RNA-seq analysis, to identify mis- or non-sense mutations accounting for the resistance. Around nine mutated genes were identified per clone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), with KCTD5 and HSD17B11 being the only mutated genes shared by more than two clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: KCTD5 and HSD17B11 are the only mutated genes shared by more than two DACR clones.
source: Around nine mutated genes were identified per clone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), with KCTD5 and HSD17B11 being the only mutated genes shared by more than two clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: KCTD5 encodes for an E3-ubiquitin ligase substrate adaptor identified as a negative regulator of the Akt pathway.
source: KCTD5 encodes for an E3-ubiquitin ligase substrate adaptor identified in a genetic screen as a negative regulator of the Akt pathway (Brockmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSD17B11 mRNA levels were strongly reduced in DACR clone #A5.
source: However, while KCTD5 mRNA was expressed in all DACR clones, HSD17B11 mRNA levels were strongly reduced in the only clone without HSD17B11 coding mutations (#A5, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Non-synonymous HSD17B11 mutations were detected in five out of six additional DACR clones.
source: To confirm this, we sequenced HSD17B11 cDNAs from six other DACR clones, and detected non-synonymous HSD17B11 mutations in five, and no HSD17B11 cDNA in the sixth, suggesting loss of expression (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from targeted sequencing, supported by data in Figure 1D, E.

claim: HSD17B11 protein was barely detectable in all the DACR clones.
source: The HSD17B11 protein was barely detectable in all the DACR clones (Figure 1F, lower band), suggesting that the mutations result in protein instability.
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting, supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: The mutations in HSD17B11 result in protein instability.
source: The HSD17B11 protein was barely detectable in all the DACR clones (Figure 1F, lower band), suggesting that the mutations result in protein instability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant protein levels are reduced.

claim: The S172 residue is critical for HSD17B11 catalysis.
source: This mutation was selected because the S172 residue is critical for catalysis (Filling et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2021), and the DACR#A4 clone, which carried S172L mutations, was the only one in which traces of full-length HSD17B11 could be detected (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: (S)–3 was ~50 times more active against cells expressing WT HSD17B11 compared to control GFP-complemented cells or cells expressing S172L HSD17B11.
source: Complemented DACR#A5 cells stably expressing WT and S172L HSD17B11-GFP at similar levels were successfully isolated (Figure 1G), and (S)–3 was ~50 times more active against cells expressing WT HSD17B11 compared to control GFP-complemented cells or cells expressing S172L HSD17B11 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from complementation experiments, supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: HSD17B11 catalytic activity is critical for (S)-DAC cytotoxicity.
source: This supports that HSD17B11 catalytic activity is critical for (S)-DAC cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation experiments showing that catalytically inactive mutant does not restore sensitivity.

claim: The DACR#A4 clone was resistant to six other cytotoxic AACs: (S)–1, (R)–1, (R)–2, (S)–4, (R,Sa)–5, and (S)–6.
source: Notably, the DACR#A4 clone (S172L mutation) was also resistant to six other cytotoxic AACs: the naturally occurring AAC (S)–1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), its synthetic enantiomer (R)–1, its shorter homologue (R)–2, the synthetic AAC (S)–4 with an internal C≡C bond and an external C=C bond (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), the allenylalkynylcarbinol (AllAC) (R,Sa)–5 (Listunov et al., 2018a) and the more cytotoxic butadiynylalkynylcarbinol (BAC) (S)–6 (Bourkhis et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: HSD17B11 functionality governs the enantiospecific cytotoxicity of the natural compound (S)–1 and all the more cytotoxic synthetic derivatives tested.
source: Thus, HSD17B11 functionality governs the enantiospecific cytotoxicity of the natural compound (S)–1 but also of all the more cytotoxic synthetic derivatives tested.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the resistance of HSD17B11 mutant clones to multiple compounds.

claim: HSD17B11 has been identified as mediating the cytotoxic effect of dehydrofalcarinol through an unknown mechanism.
source: In addition, HSD17B11 has been recently identified as mediating, through an unknown mechanism, the cytotoxic effect of dehydrofalcarinol, a polyacetylenic compound with a terminal butadiynylalkenylcarbinol motif isolated from several plants of the Asteraceae family (Grant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study, supported by citation.

claim: HSD17B11 uses NAD+ to catalyze oxidation of the C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to generate androsterone.
source: HSD17B11, also called SDR16C2 [Persson et al., 2009], PAN1B, DHRS8, or retSDR2, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lipid droplets (LD) via a N-terminal targeting domain (Figure 1E), where it uses NAD+ to catalyze oxidation of the C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to generate androsterone, a weak androgen (Brereton et al., 2001; Horiguchi et al., 2008a) (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HSD17B11 localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lipid droplets (LD) via a N-terminal targeting domain.
source: HSD17B11, also called SDR16C2 [Persson et al., 2009], PAN1B, DHRS8, or retSDR2, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lipid droplets (LD) via a N-terminal targeting domain (Figure 1E), where it uses NAD+ to catalyze oxidation of the C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to generate androsterone, a weak androgen (Brereton et al., 2001; Horiguchi et al., 2008a) (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Androsterone is a weak androgen.
source: HSD17B11, also called SDR16C2 [Persson et al., 2009], PAN1B, DHRS8, or retSDR2, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and lipid droplets (LD) via a N-terminal targeting domain (Figure 1E), where it uses NAD+ to catalyze oxidation of the C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol to generate androsterone, a weak androgen (Brereton et al., 2001; Horiguchi et al., 2008a) (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol has the same spatial orientation as the (S)–3 carbinol when its lipidic chain is superimposed with the C13(C18) side of the steroid skeleton.
source: The C17 carbinol center of androstan-3-alpha,17-beta-diol, which is naturally oxidized by HSD17B11 (Figure 2; Brereton et al., 2001), has the same spatial orientation as the (S)–3 carbinol when its lipidic chain is superimposed with the C13(C18) side of the steroid skeleton (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on molecular modeling.

claim: When the DACone 7 was previously synthesized and tested, no cytotoxic activity was found.
source: However, when the DACone 7 was previously synthesized and tested, no cytotoxic activity was found (Listunov et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Medium components such as serum albumin may rapidly react with and inactivate DACones.
source: Given the high in vitro electrophilic reactivity of ynones as Michael acceptors of thiols and amines (Worch et al., 2021), we considered that medium components such as serum albumin may rapidly react with and inactivate DACones.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known chemical reactivity of ynones.

claim: DACones 7 and 8 are cytotoxic in the absence of serum.
source: To test this, we synthesized the DACone 7, as well as a homologue with a shorter alkyl chain 8, and treated U2OS cells in a protein-free medium (PBS containing CaCl2 and MgCl2 to maintain cellular adhesion). Both the DACones 7 and 8 were indeed cytotoxic in the absence of serum, with 8 (short chain) being even more active than (S)–3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays in protein-free medium, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: DACone 8 is more cytotoxic than (S)–3 in the absence of serum.
source: Both the DACones 7 and 8 were indeed cytotoxic in the absence of serum, with 8 (short chain) being even more active than (S)–3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The cytotoxicity of DACones 7 and 8 is not affected by inactivation of HSD17B11.
source: While the cytotoxicity of (S)–3 was strongly reduced by inactivation of HSD17B11, the cytotoxicity of the DACones 7 and 8 was not affected, supporting the notion that the DACones are the cytotoxic products generated from DACs by HSD17B11.
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays comparing wild-type and HSD17B11-deficient cells.

claim: DACones are the cytotoxic products generated from DACs by HSD17B11.
source: While the cytotoxicity of (S)–3 was strongly reduced by inactivation of HSD17B11, the cytotoxicity of the DACones 7 and 8 was not affected, supporting the notion that the DACones are the cytotoxic products generated from DACs by HSD17B11.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of HSD17B11 inactivation on DACs vs DACones.

claim: Covalent adducts are formed on BSA with DACone 10 but not with (S)–9.
source: The clickable DACone 10, or clickable DAC (S)–9 as control, were incubated with fetal bovine serum (FBS) or purified bovine serum albumin (BSA), followed by CuAAC-mediated ligation of an AlexaFluor647-azido fluorophore to the free C≡CH tag. The proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and scanned for fluorescence (Speers and Cravatt, 2004). Covalent adducts were formed on BSA with DACone 10 but not with (S)–9 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from click chemistry experiments, supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: DACone 10 reacts with several model proteins, including bovine beta-lactoglobuline (BLG).
source: Moreover, the DACone 10 also reacted with several other model proteins, including the bovine beta-lactoglobuline (BLG) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from click chemistry experiments, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DACone adducts are produced only when using the clickable DACones 10 or 11.
source: Using BSA and BLG, we established that DACone adducts are produced only when using the clickable DACones 10 or 11 (Figure 2E), suggesting that the terminal triple bond of the DACone pharmacophore is modified or masked after reaction.
evidence: This is a finding from click chemistry experiments, supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The terminal triple bond of the DACone pharmacophore is modified or masked after reaction.
source: Using BSA and BLG, we established that DACone adducts are produced only when using the clickable DACones 10 or 11 (Figure 2E), suggesting that the terminal triple bond of the DACone pharmacophore is modified or masked after reaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only clickable DACones produce adducts.

claim: Immunopurified WT HSD17B11 activates (S)–9, but not (R)–9, into BLG-reactive species.
source: Finally, we could recapitulate the activation of (S)–9, but not of (R)–9, into protein-reactive species by immunopurified WT HSD17B11, but not by the S172L mutant (Figure 2F), supporting an enantiospecific bioactivation of (S)–9 into the BLG-reactive DACone 10 by HSD17B11.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro bioactivation assays, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: The S172L mutant of HSD17B11 does not activate (S)–9 into BLG-reactive species.
source: Finally, we could recapitulate the activation of (S)–9, but not of (R)–9, into protein-reactive species by immunopurified WT HSD17B11, but not by the S172L mutant (Figure 2F), supporting an enantiospecific bioactivation of (S)–9 into the BLG-reactive DACone 10 by HSD17B11.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro bioactivation assays, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: HSD17B11 enantiospecifically oxidizes (S)–3 into the DACone 7.
source: Considering that HSD17B11 known activity is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of a secondary carbinol into a ketone and that the only hydroxyl group on (S)–3 is the one occurring in the dialkynylcarbinol pharmacophore, this experiment strongly supports the notion that HSD17B11 enantiospecifically oxidizes (S)–3 into the DACone 7, which immediately reacts with nearby proteins, including HSD17B11-GFP itself as observed in Figure 2F.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on enzymatic activity and in vitro bioactivation experiments.

claim: DACone 7 immediately reacts with nearby proteins, including HSD17B11-GFP itself.
source: Considering that HSD17B11 known activity is the NAD+-dependent oxidation of a secondary carbinol into a ketone and that the only hydroxyl group on (S)–3 is the one occurring in the dialkynylcarbinol pharmacophore, this experiment strongly supports the notion that HSD17B11 enantiospecifically oxidizes (S)–3 into the DACone 7, which immediately reacts with nearby proteins, including HSD17B11-GFP itself as observed in Figure 2F.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro bioactivation assays, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: Both (S)–3 and (R)–3 docked into the catalytic cavity of HSD17B11.
source: Both (S)–3 and (R)–3 docked into the catalytic cavity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), but (R)–3 had a lower computed affinity than (S)–3 (155 nM vs 15 nM) and only (S)–3 had its hydroxyl group properly positioned to engage hydrogen bonds with the S172 and Y185 catalytic amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E), which is critical for further carbinol oxidation via hydride transfer to NAD+ (Filling et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from molecular docking studies, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: (R)–3 has a lower computed affinity for HSD17B11 than (S)–3 (155 nM vs 15 nM).
source: Both (S)–3 and (R)–3 docked into the catalytic cavity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), but (R)–3 had a lower computed affinity than (S)–3 (155 nM vs 15 nM) and only (S)–3 had its hydroxyl group properly positioned to engage hydrogen bonds with the S172 and Y185 catalytic amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E), which is critical for further carbinol oxidation via hydride transfer to NAD+ (Filling et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from molecular docking studies.

claim: Only (S)–3 has its hydroxyl group properly positioned to engage hydrogen bonds with the S172 and Y185 catalytic amino acids of HSD17B11.
source: Both (S)–3 and (R)–3 docked into the catalytic cavity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), but (R)–3 had a lower computed affinity than (S)–3 (155 nM vs 15 nM) and only (S)–3 had its hydroxyl group properly positioned to engage hydrogen bonds with the S172 and Y185 catalytic amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E), which is critical for further carbinol oxidation via hydride transfer to NAD+ (Filling et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from molecular docking studies, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: Hydrogen bonding with S172 and Y185 is critical for carbinol oxidation via hydride transfer to NAD+.
source: Both (S)–3 and (R)–3 docked into the catalytic cavity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), but (R)–3 had a lower computed affinity than (S)–3 (155 nM vs 15 nM) and only (S)–3 had its hydroxyl group properly positioned to engage hydrogen bonds with the S172 and Y185 catalytic amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E), which is critical for further carbinol oxidation via hydride transfer to NAD+ (Filling et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: (S)–3 docked onto the catalytic domains of HSD17B13 and HSD17B3 in addition to HSD17B11.
source: This filtering revealed that, beyond HSD17B11, (S)–3 also docked onto the catalytic domains of only two 17β-HSDs, HSD17B13 and HSD17B3, while (R)–3 docked onto two different 17β-HSDs, HSD17B9 and HSD17B6.
evidence: This is a finding from molecular docking studies on multiple SDRs.

claim: (R)–3 docked onto the catalytic domains of HSD17B9 and HSD17B6.
source: This filtering revealed that, beyond HSD17B11, (S)–3 also docked onto the catalytic domains of only two 17β-HSDs, HSD17B13 and HSD17B3, while (R)–3 docked onto two different 17β-HSDs, HSD17B9 and HSD17B6.
evidence: This is a finding from molecular docking studies on multiple SDRs.

claim: HSD17B3 is a reductive SDR involved in testosterone biosynthesis.
source: HSD17B3 (aka EDH17B3 or SDR12C2 [Persson et al., 2009]) is a reductive SDR involved in testosterone biosynthesisso it was not tested further.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSD17B3.

claim: HSD17B13 is an oxidative SDR and the closest homologue of HSD17B11.
source: In contrast, since HSD17B13 (aka SCDR9 or SDR16C3 [Persson et al., 2009]), whose expression is restricted to the liver, is an oxidative SDR, the closest homologue of HSD17B11 and is also localized at the ER (Horiguchi et al., 2008b), we tested whether it could complement U2OS KO for HSD17B11.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSD17B13, supported by citations.

claim: HSD17B13 expression is restricted to the liver.
source: In contrast, since HSD17B13 (aka SCDR9 or SDR16C3 [Persson et al., 2009]), whose expression is restricted to the liver, is an oxidative SDR, the closest homologue of HSD17B11 and is also localized at the ER (Horiguchi et al., 2008b), we tested whether it could complement U2OS KO for HSD17B11.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSD17B13.

claim: HSD17B13 is localized at the ER.
source: In contrast, since HSD17B13 (aka SCDR9 or SDR16C3 [Persson et al., 2009]), whose expression is restricted to the liver, is an oxidative SDR, the closest homologue of HSD17B11 and is also localized at the ER (Horiguchi et al., 2008b), we tested whether it could complement U2OS KO for HSD17B11.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HSD17B13 is able to bioactivate (S)–3 into cytotoxic compounds, albeit less efficiently than HSD17B11.
source: This revealed that HSD17B13 is also able to bioactivate (S)–3 into cytotoxic compounds, albeit in a less efficient manner as compared to HSD17B11 (IC50 of 30 nM vs 12 nM for HSD17B11 with similar complementation levels, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from complementation experiments, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G, H.

claim: Both BLG isoforms were completely modified by DACone 10 with the formation of one or two adducts of ~+242 Da.
source: Purified BLG contains two isoforms (A and B, differing by 86.0 Da) and, when incubated with DACone, both BLG isoforms were completely modified with the formation of one or two adducts of ~+242 Da (Figure 2G), which corresponds to the mass of the clickable DACone 10.
evidence: This is a finding from mass spectrometry analysis, supported by data in Figure 2G.

claim: BLG gains an absorption band at ~323 nm upon modification by DACone.
source: Monitoring the absorbance spectra of modified BLG revealed that BLG gains an absorption band at ~323 nm upon modification by DACone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from UV-visible spectroscopy, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both BLG and BSA are modified by the DACones 7 and 8 or their clickable analogues 10 and 11.
source: Using this, we confirmed that both BLG and BSA are modified by the DACones 7 and 8 or their clickable analogues 10 and 11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from UV-visible spectroscopy, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The shorter DACone 8 is more reactive than DACone 7, in line with its greater cytotoxicity.
source: The shorter DACone 8 proved to be even more reactive, in line with its greater cytotoxicity (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from reactivity and cytotoxicity assays, supported by data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: DACones 10 and 11 react with cysteine and lysine side chains in proteins.
source: This revealed that both DACones reacted with cysteine and lysine side chains, with the expected modification being detected ( + 729.4498/ + 723.4408 Da (Heavy/Light) for DACone 10, + 631.3404/ + 625.3332 Da (Heavy/Light) for DACone 11, Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, F, Supplementary file 1A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from isoDTB-ABPP chemoproteomics, supported by data in Figure 2H and supplementary files.

claim: DACone-modified lysines are preferentially surrounded by hydrophobic amino acids.
source: Accordingly, analysis of the sequence context of the amino acids identified as modified by the DACone 10 revealed an enrichment of hydrophobic amino acids around the modified lysines, which was not observed for the modified cysteines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis of modified sites, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: At neutral pH, DACones only react with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) but not with Nα-acetyl-L-lysine (NAK).
source: We next confirmed the reactivity of DACones with cysteine and lysine side chains by monitoring the appearance of the ~323 nm absorbance band after reaction of the DACone 8 with isolated amino acids, using N-acetylated versions to prevent reactions with the N-terminal amino group. At neutral pH, DACones only reacted with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) but not with Nα-acetyl-L-lysine (NAK) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, left spectrum), whereas at higher pH they reacted with both NAC and NAK (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, right spectrum), in agreement with the nucleophilic reactivity of the non-protonated ε−NH2 group of the lysine chain.
evidence: This is a finding from UV-visible spectroscopy of reactions with isolated amino acids, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: At higher pH, DACones react with both NAC and NAK.
source: At neutral pH, DACones only reacted with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) but not with Nα-acetyl-L-lysine (NAK) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, left spectrum), whereas at higher pH they reacted with both NAC and NAK (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, right spectrum), in agreement with the nucleophilic reactivity of the non-protonated ε−NH2 group of the lysine chain.
evidence: This is a finding from UV-visible spectroscopy, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The DACone 8-NAK linkage is progressively lost when incubated in 0.1% TFA (38% reduction after 1 h incubation).
source: By monitoring the adducts absorbance, we confirmed that the DACone 8-NAK linkage is progressively lost when incubated in 0.1% TFA (38% reduction after 1 h incubation), while the DACone 8-NAC linkage remains unaffected in these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is a finding from stability assays, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: The DACone 8-NAC linkage remains unaffected when incubated in 0.1% TFA.
source: By monitoring the adducts absorbance, we confirmed that the DACone 8-NAK linkage is progressively lost when incubated in 0.1% TFA (38% reduction after 1 h incubation), while the DACone 8-NAC linkage remains unaffected in these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is a finding from stability assays, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: The reactivity with lysine side chains is underestimated by the isoDTB-ABPP experiment due to preferential loss of the lysine-DACone species.
source: These data suggest that the reactivity with lysine side chains is underestimated by our isoDTB-ABPP experiment due to preferential loss of the lysine-DACone species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed instability of lysine-DACone adducts under acidic conditions.

claim: A covalent bond forms by addition of the thiol (NAC) or amino (NAK) group onto the terminal alkyne of the DACone head.
source: Using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), we characterized the products of the reaction of the short DACone 8 with NAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B) or NAK (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D). This revealed that a covalent bond forms by addition of the thiol (NAC) or amino (NAK) group onto the terminal alkyne of the DACone head (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from NMR characterization, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-E.

claim: A similar reaction occurs with the cysteine and lysine residues of proteins.
source: A similar reaction probably occurs with the cysteine and lysine residues of proteins, which is supported by their gain of a similar absorbance band upon treatment with DACone (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of spectroscopic properties between model compounds and proteins.

claim: DACones immediately react with nearby proteins which limits the activity of general detoxification mechanisms.
source: However, the fact that modulating glutathione levels or GST activity in cells only had a very small impact on (S)-DAC cytotoxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E) indicates that, once produced, DACones immediately react with nearby proteins which limits the activity of general detoxification mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments showing limited effect of glutathione modulation, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: The cytotoxicity of the clickable DAC 9 is enantiospecific, biased toward (S)–9, and dependent on bioactivation by HSD17B11.
source: As observed for the DAC 3, the cytotoxicity of the clickable DAC 9 was enantiospecific, biased toward (S)–9, and dependent on bioactivation by HSD17B11 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Multiple modified proteins were detected in extracts from (S)–9-treated cells, while no adduct with (R)–9 was detected.
source: Cells were treated with clickable (S)- or (R)–9 DACs, extracts prepared and click chemistry used to detect the covalent adducts of DACs onto proteins (Speers and Cravatt, 2004). Multiple modified proteins were detected in extracts from (S)–9-treated cells, while no adduct with (R)–9 was detected (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from click chemistry experiments, supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Forty-two proteins were significantly enriched more than 2-fold in the (S)–9 condition as compared to (R)–9.
source: Forty-two proteins were significantly enriched more than 2-fold in the (S)–9 condition as compared to (R)–9 (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3), with three proteins being enriched more than 60-fold: BRAT1, PLIN3, and PSMD2.
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis, supported by data in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: BRAT1, PLIN3, and PSMD2 were enriched more than 60-fold in the (S)–9 condition.
source: Forty-two proteins were significantly enriched more than 2-fold in the (S)–9 condition as compared to (R)–9 (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3), with three proteins being enriched more than 60-fold: BRAT1, PLIN3, and PSMD2.
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis, supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: BRAT1, PSMD2, and PLIN3 are robustly modified by (S)–9 but not by (R)–9 in cells.
source: To validate that the three most highly enriched hits are modified in cells, we overexpressed BRAT1, PSMD2 and PLIN3 individually (in addition to TK1) as GFP fusions in U2OS cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), and used GFP pull-down to determine whether they were modified by clickable DAC 9 in cells. These proteins were found robustly modified by (S)–9 but not by (R)–9, especially BRAT1 and PSMD2, while GFP alone was not modified (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from validation experiments, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Only 42 proteins were found robustly and reproducibly enriched with (S)–9 over (R)–9 in cells, indicating a certain degree of selectivity for protein modification by DACones.
source: The fact that only 42 proteins were found robustly and reproducibly enriched with (S)–9 over (R)–9 in cells indicates a certain degree of selectivity for protein modification by DACones that could result from its production and reactivity being restricted to the vicinity of HSD17B11.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the proteomics data.

claim: DACones rapidly and selectively react with a specific set of proteins in the vicinity of HSD17B11.
source: These data suggest that DACones rapidly and selectively react with a specific set of proteins in the vicinity of HSD17B11 as shown for another in situ generated electrophile (Paxman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the limited number of modified proteins and comparison to literature.

claim: PSMD2 is an essential protein in HAP-1 cells.
source: Among the three main hits, PSMD2 drew our attention as an essential protein in HAP-1 cells (Blomen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PSMD2 is a critical non-catalytic subunit of the 19 S regulatory particle of the 26 S proteasome.
source: PSMD2, also called Rpn1, is a critical non-catalytic subunit of the 19 S regulatory particle of the 26 S proteasome, a large complex responsible for the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of cellular proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSMD2 function.

claim: PSMD2 is essential for 19 S assembly and for docking of ubiquitin, ubiquitin receptors and the deubiquitinase USP14.
source: PSMD2 is essential for 19 S assembly and for docking of ubiquitin, ubiquitin receptors and the deubiquitinase USP14 (Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Endogenous PSMD2 is covalently modified after treatment with the DAC (S)–9 but not with (R)–9.
source: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous PSMD2 from U2OS cells treated with clickable DAC confirmed that PSMD2 is covalently modified after treatment with the DAC (S)–9 but not with (R)–9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation experiments, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The clickable DACone 10 efficiently modifies PSMD2 in vitro.
source: Moreover, the clickable DACone 10 efficiently modified PSMD2 in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro modification assays, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The modification of cellular proteins by (S)–9, including PSMD2, is dependent on HSD17B11.
source: Using the (S)-DAC-resistant HAP-1 clones A1 and A4 (expressing V16D and S172L HSD17B11 mutants, respectively), we also confirmed that the modification of cellular proteins by (S)–9, including PSMD2, was dependent on HSD17B11 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with resistant clones, supported by data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: A cluster of proteins involved in protein quality control (PQC) is modified by the DAC (S)–9.
source: Our proteomics approach also revealed that, in addition to PSMD2, a cluster of proteins involved in protein quality control (PQC) was also modified by the DAC (S)–9 (Figure 3B), including several protein disulfide isomerases (P4HB/PDIA1, PDIA6 and TMX1), thioredoxin reductases (TXNDC5 and TXNRD1) and protein chaperones (the ER-resident HSP70, HSPA5/GRP78/BiP; and HSP90AB1), the alteration of which likely also contributes to the DAC cytotoxic effect.
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis, supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: (S)-DACs are bioactivated by HSD7B11 into highly reactive DACones that covalently lipoxidize nearby proteins, including essential proteins involved in PQC such as PSMD2.
source: Altogether, these data show that (S)-DACs are bioactivated by HSD7B11 into highly reactive DACones that covalently lipoxidize nearby proteins, including essential proteins involved in PQC such as PSMD2, a critical subunit of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: (S)–9 gives a strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining evocative of ER and mitochondrial membranes.
source: We then used click-based imaging to monitor the localization of DAC-modified proteins. (S)–9 gave a strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining, the latter being evocative of ER and mitochondrial membranes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from click-based imaging, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a co-occurrence of (S)–9-click staining with markers of ER and mitochondria.
source: In agreement, we observed a co-occurrence of (S)–9-click staining with markers of ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and mitochondria (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from co-localization imaging, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: The lack of staining in cells treated with (R)–9 supports that the staining corresponds to DAC-modified proteins.
source: The lack of staining in cells treated with the inactive (R)–9 (Figure 3E) supported that the staining corresponds to DAC-modified proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: No staining was observed with (S)–3, supporting that the -C≡CH group of the dialkynylcarbinol head is modified after bioactivation and subsequent reaction with proteins.
source: No staining was observed with (S)–3, supporting that the -C≡CH group of the dialkynylcarbinol head is modified after bioactivation and subsequent reaction with proteins (as shown in Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data, supported by reference to Figure 2I.

claim: GFP-BRAT1 is retained to subcellular compartments evocative of ER and nucleus after treatment with (S)–3.
source: Since GFP-BRAT1 is the protein that was the most robustly modified by DACs in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), we pre-extracted soluble proteins with mild nonionic detergent to assess GFP-BRAT1 association to subcellular compartments. Under these conditions, most GFP-BRAT1 was removed by the pre-extraction in untreated cells, as expected for a soluble protein, while it was retained to subcellular compartments evocative of ER and nucleus after treatment with (S)–3 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from pre-extraction and imaging experiments, supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Protein lipoxidation by bioactivated DACs results in relocalization of some proteins to cellular membranes.
source: These data suggest that protein lipoxidation by bioactivated DACs results, at least for some of them, into their relocalization to cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the imaging data showing membrane association of modified proteins.

claim: Treatment of cells by (S)–3 triggers ER swelling as shown by the appearance of a large cytoplasmic vacuole between 4 and 8 h of treatment that preceded cell death.
source: In agreement with (S)-DAC impairing PQC, we observed that treatment of cells by (S)–3 triggers ER swelling as shown by the appearance of a large cytoplasmic vacuole between 4 and 8 h of treatment that preceded cell death (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging, supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: The vacuoles observed after (S)–3 treatment derive from the ER.
source: The use of a GFP variant targeted and retained into the ER confirmed that these vacuoles derived from this compartment (Figure 4B), while a mCherry protein addressed to mitochondria in the same cells showed that (S)-DAC treatment concomitantly triggered mitochondrial fission, a hallmark of cell stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see also Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging with ER marker, supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: (S)-DAC treatment triggers mitochondrial fission, a hallmark of cell stress.
source: The use of a GFP variant targeted and retained into the ER confirmed that these vacuoles derived from this compartment (Figure 4B), while a mCherry protein addressed to mitochondria in the same cells showed that (S)-DAC treatment concomitantly triggered mitochondrial fission, a hallmark of cell stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see also Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from live imaging with mitochondrial marker, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Video 1.

claim: ER swelling is a feature of ER-stress.
source: ER swelling is a feature of ER-stress, which can result from the accumulation of unfolded proteins within the ER and can be triggered by various defects of PQC such as inhibition of the UPS, as seen with the UPS inhibitor MG132 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ER-stress, with supporting data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Vacuolization and cell death induced by (S)–3 can be blocked by inhibition of protein synthesis by cycloheximide.
source: In agreement with (S)–3 cytotoxicity being mediated by the accumulation of unfolded proteins, vacuolization and cell death induced by (S)–3 could be blocked by inhibition of protein synthesis by cycloheximide (CHX, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with cycloheximide, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: (S)–3 triggers a strong accumulation of the chaperone HSP70 and of the cell stress response protein p21, similarly to MG132.
source: (S)–3 also triggered a strong accumulation of the chaperone HSP70 and of the cell stress response protein p21, similarly to MG132 (Figure 4C) or PSMD2 depletion using siRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting, supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ER-stress can trigger UPS inhibition, likely through consuming free ubiquitin.
source: It is noteworthy that ER-stress itself can trigger UPS inhibition, likely through consuming free ubiquitin (Menéndez-Benito et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: (S)–3 induces the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins, a hallmark of UPS inhibition.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we observed that (S)–3 induces the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 4D), a hallmark of UPS inhibition, and blocked the degradation of an artificial substrate of the UPS system in a manner similar to MG132 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting, supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: (S)–3 blocks the degradation of an artificial substrate of the UPS system in a manner similar to MG132.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we observed that (S)–3 induces the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 4D), a hallmark of UPS inhibition, and blocked the degradation of an artificial substrate of the UPS system in a manner similar to MG132 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from UPS reporter assays, supported by data in Figure 4E and F.

claim: (S)–3 blocks the assembly of the protein 53BP1 into foci at sites of DNA double-strand breaks.
source: Similarly to MG132, (S)–3 also blocked the assembly of the protein 53BP1 into foci at sites of DNA double-strand breaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), a process that depends on the local de novo DNA damage-induced ubiquitination of histones (Mailand et al., 2007), thereby confirming depletion of free ubiquitin by treatment with (S)–3.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: (S)–3 treatment itself did not induce DNA damage nor blocked ATM activation.
source: It is noteworthy that (S)–3 treatment itself did not induce DNA damage nor blocked ATM activation, an important component of the DNA damage response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence and immunoblotting, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The UPR aims at restoring ER protein homeostasis by reducing the influx of proteins into the ER and by increasing the activity of ER protein quality control mechanisms.
source: Accumulation of unfolded proteins in the ER activates three ER-resident transmembrane signal transducers: the IRE1α kinase/endoribonuclease, the PERK kinase and the ATF6 transcription factor, which represent the three arms of the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR). The UPR aims at restoring ER protein homeostasis by reducing the influx of proteins into the ER and by increasing the activity of ER protein quality control mechanisms (Preissler and Ron, 2019; Szegezdi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the UPR, supported by citations.

claim: IRE1α activation is marked by its autophosphorylation on S724 and the processing of the XBP-1 mRNA resulting in the production of the XBP1-s transcription factor.
source: IRE1α activation is marked by its autophosphorylation on S724 and the processing of the XBP-1 mRNA resulting in the production of the XBP1-s transcription factor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IRE1α activation.

claim: PERK activation is marked by its autophosphorylation on T980 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α S51, which reduces translation initiation and triggers the accumulation of the ATF4 transcription factor.
source: PERK activation is marked by its autophosphorylation on T980 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α S51, which reduces translation initiation and triggers the accumulation of the ATF4 transcription factor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PERK activation.

claim: ATF6 activation relies on its cleavage which releases a short-lived transcriptionally active fragment.
source: ATF6 activation relies on its cleavage which releases a short-lived transcriptionally active fragment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATF6 activation.

claim: Persistent UPR activation can promote apoptosis in a JNK-dependent manner.
source: Persistent UPR activation can promote apoptosis in a JNK-dependent manner (Szegezdi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Treatment with (S)–3 induces the activation of the three UPR pathways with the rapid phosphorylation of IRE1α (S724), PERK (T980) and eIF2α (S51), a strong decrease of full-length ATF6, preceding the accumulation of cytoplasmic HSP70 and the transient accumulation of XBP-1s and ATF4.
source: In agreement with (S)–3 triggering unfolded proteins accumulation and UPR activation, we observed that treatment with (S)–3 induced the activation of the three UPR pathways with the rapid phosphorylation of IRE1α (S724), PERK (T980) and eIF2α (S51), a strong decrease of full-length ATF6, preceding the accumulation of cytoplasmic HSP70 and the transient accumulation of XBP-1s and ATF4 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting of UPR markers, supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Treatment with inhibitors of either IRE1α endoribonuclease, IRE1α kinase or PERK did not modify the toxicity of (S)–3.
source: Of note, treatment with inhibitors of either IRE1α endoribonuclease, IRE1α kinase or PERK did not modify the toxicity of (S)–3, suggesting that the ER stress induced by (S)–3 is too acute to be resolved in a timely manner by the UPR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays with UPR inhibitors, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The ER stress induced by (S)–3 is too acute to be resolved in a timely manner by the UPR.
source: Of note, treatment with inhibitors of either IRE1α endoribonuclease, IRE1α kinase or PERK did not modify the toxicity of (S)–3, suggesting that the ER stress induced by (S)–3 is too acute to be resolved in a timely manner by the UPR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of effect of UPR inhibitors.

claim: JNK inhibition provides a small degree of resistance to (S)–3 (IC50 shift from 33 to 70 nM).
source: In contrast, JNK inhibition provided a small degree of resistance to (S)–3 (IC50 shift from 33 to 70 nM), suggesting a contribution of the JNK pathway to cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays with JNK inhibitor, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The JNK pathway contributes to cell death induced by (S)–3.
source: In contrast, JNK inhibition provided a small degree of resistance to (S)–3 (IC50 shift from 33 to 70 nM), suggesting a contribution of the JNK pathway to cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial rescue by JNK inhibition.

claim: (S)–3 treatment results in apoptosis, as marked by PARP-1 cleavage.
source: Ultimately, (S)–3 treatment resulted in apoptosis, as marked by PARP-1 cleavage (Figure 4G), in a caspase inhibitor (z-VAD-fmk)-sensitive manner (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblotting of apoptosis markers, supported by data in Figure 4G.

claim: Apoptosis induced by (S)–3 is caspase-dependent.
source: Ultimately, (S)–3 treatment resulted in apoptosis, as marked by PARP-1 cleavage (Figure 4G), in a caspase inhibitor (z-VAD-fmk)-sensitive manner (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with caspase inhibitor, supported by data in Figure 4H.

claim: Caspase inhibition blocks cell death but not the vacuolization process induced by (S)–3.
source: Caspase inhibition blocked cell death but not the vacuolization process (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from imaging with caspase inhibitor, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: (S)–3, once bioactivated by HSD17B11, covalently modifies multiple proteins including critical components of the PQC, resulting in ER-stress, activation of the UPR and inhibition of the UPS, ultimately leading to apoptotic cell death.
source: Altogether, these results show that (S)–3, once bioactivated by HSD17B11, covalently modifies multiple proteins including critical components of the PQC, resulting in ER-stress, activation of the UPR and inhibition of the UPS, ultimately leading to apoptotic cell death.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The AAC (S)–4 still retains some cytotoxicity (IC50 ~2.6 µM) on DAC-resistant clone A4.
source: We found that the AAC (S)–4 (with a terminal C=CH2 group, Figure 5A), despite its activity being strongly reduced in DAC-resistant clone A4 (~17-fold, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), still retained some cytotoxicity (IC50 ~2.6 µM) on these cells, possibly through bioactivation by a second dehydrogenase.
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The RDH11 gene carries point mutations in five out of seven AACR clones.
source: Among those, we selected seven, which all showed similar increased resistance to (S)–4 (Figure 5A), and submitted them to RNA-seq analysis. This allowed the identification of an average of six coding mutations in each clone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and analysis revealed that the RDH11 gene carried point mutations in five of these seven clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: RDH11 expression was severely downregulated in the AACR clone B4.
source: Further analysis revealed that the clone A6 contained two alleles of RDH11, each with a different point mutation (Figure 5B), and RDH11 expression was severely downregulated in the clone B4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The RDH11 gene was mutated or downregulated in all the AACR clones.
source: In conclusion, the RDH11 gene was mutated (Figure 5C) or downregulated in all the AACR clones, implicating it as an SDR, with similar prodrug bioactivation capacity as HSD17B11, that mediates AAC (S)–4 toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and expression data.

claim: RDH11 is an SDR with similar prodrug bioactivation capacity as HSD17B11 that mediates AAC (S)–4 toxicity.

claim: RDH11 codes for retinol dehydrogenase 11, a member of the SDR superfamily which localizes to the ER.
source: The human RDH11 gene codes for retinol dehydrogenase 11 (also called SDR7C1 [Persson et al., 2009], PSDR1 or HSD17B15), a member of the SDR superfamily which also localizes to the ER (Kedishvili et al., 2002) where it uses NADP+ to catalyze the conversion of retinol (Figure 5D, preferentially the 11-cis, all-trans and 9-cis isomers) into retinal through oxidation of the C-15 carbinol center, with a pro-R hydrogen specificity (Haeseleer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RDH11, supported by citations.

claim: RDH11 uses NADP+ to catalyze the conversion of retinol into retinal through oxidation of the C-15 carbinol center, with a pro-R hydrogen specificity.
source: The human RDH11 gene codes for retinol dehydrogenase 11 (also called SDR7C1 [Persson et al., 2009], PSDR1 or HSD17B15), a member of the SDR superfamily which also localizes to the ER (Kedishvili et al., 2002) where it uses NADP+ to catalyze the conversion of retinol (Figure 5D, preferentially the 11-cis, all-trans and 9-cis isomers) into retinal through oxidation of the C-15 carbinol center, with a pro-R hydrogen specificity (Haeseleer et al., 2002).

claim: HSD17B11 is responsible for the nM activity of the AAC (S)–4 (48-fold IC50 increase as a result of HSD17B11 inactivation).
source: In this panel, we confirmed that, while HSD17B11 was responsible for the nM activity of the AAC (S)–4 (48-fold IC50 increase as a result of HSD17B11 inactivation), the remaining toxicity of (S)–4 in HSD17B11 KO cells was further decreased by inactivating RDH11 (sixfold IC50 increase by RDH11 inactivation, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays with knockout cells, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The remaining toxicity of (S)–4 in HSD17B11 KO cells is further decreased by inactivating RDH11 (sixfold IC50 increase by RDH11 inactivation).
source: In this panel, we confirmed that, while HSD17B11 was responsible for the nM activity of the AAC (S)–4 (48-fold IC50 increase as a result of HSD17B11 inactivation), the remaining toxicity of (S)–4 in HSD17B11 KO cells was further decreased by inactivating RDH11 (sixfold IC50 increase by RDH11 inactivation, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).

claim: RDH11 bioactivates preferentially (S)–4 (IC50~0.28 µM) over (S)–3 (IC50~1.92 µM).

evidence: This is a finding from complementation experiments, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: HSD17B11 is much more efficient than RDH11 for the bioactivation of (S)–3 and (S)–4 (IC50 < 40 nM).
source: Comparison of the activity of (S)–3 and (S)–4 on U2OS KO [HSD17B11 + RDH11] complemented either by HSD17B11-GFP or RDH11 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) revealed that RDH11 bioactivates preferentially (S)–4 (IC50~0.28 µM, with a terminal C=CH2 group) over (S)–3 (IC50~1.92 µM, with a terminal C≡CH group, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), but also established that HSD17B11 was much more efficient than RDH11 for the bioactivation of either molecule (IC50 < 40 nM).
evidence: This is a finding from complementation experiments, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Introduction of a second secondary carbinol function in the AAC structure generates the AlkenylAlkynylDiCarbinol 12 (AADC), which is equally bioactivated by HSD17B11 and RDH11.
source: Introduction of a second secondary carbinol function in the AAC structure, generating the AlkenylAlkynylDiCarbinol 12 (AADC), reduced its bioactivation by HSD17B11, while leaving intact its RDH11-dependent activation and thereby generating a new prodrug equally bioactivated by HSD17B11 and RDH11 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays with a new compound, supported by data in Figure 5G.

claim: HPGD is responsible for the inactivation of prostaglandins through oxidation of the (S)-C-15 carbinol center in a NAD+-dependent manner.

claim: HPGD expression is tissue-restricted (prostate and bladder) and null in U2OS cells.
source: HPGD expression is tissue-restricted (prostate and bladder) and null in U2OS cells (Broad Institute Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia RNA-seq dataset).

claim: The AllAC (S,Sa)–5 is selectively bioactivated by HPGD, resulting in an IC50 of ~147 nM in HPGD-overexpressing cells vs normal U2OS.
source: To determine whether this SDR could also bioactivate potential prodrugs, we used U2OS inactivated for HSD17B11 and overexpressing GFP alone or HPGD-GFP (Figure 5I), and screened a small collection of lipidic alkynylcarbinols. We found that the AllAC (S,Sa)–5 was selectively bioactivated by HPGD, resulting in an IC50 of ~147 nM in HPGD-overexpressing cells vs normal U2OS (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a finding from cell viability assays with HPGD overexpression, supported by data in Figure 5J.
